claims.text: A low-carbon, high-strength tempered martensitic steel can exhibit a full ductile–brittle–ductile transition under precisely controlled heat-treatment conditions.
The proposed tempered martensitic steel is a well-studied material system.
Brittle behavior at intermediate treatment temperatures is caused by temper embrittlement.
Segregation of impurities at grain boundaries is a mechanism of the proposed intermediate-temperature embrittlement.
Re-entrant ductility at higher treatment temperatures results from diffusion-mediated homogenization or coarsening of embrittling features.
Standard quenching and tempering produces the proposed tempered martensitic steel initial state.
The initial microstructure is ductile at low temperatures.
The relevant temper-embrittlement treatment window is narrow and may lie approximately between 300 and 500 °C, depending on alloy composition.
Treatment at temperatures above the embrittlement window can provide sufficient diffusion to recover ductility.
Impurity elements such as phosphorus reversibly segregate to grain boundaries and subsequently re-diffuse or coarsen.
Grain-boundary impurity segregation causes intergranular embrittlement.
Higher atomic mobility at elevated temperatures re-homogenizes segregated species or forms or coarsens secondary phases.
Re-homogenization or secondary-phase coarsening reduces the embrittling effect and restores ductile behavior.
The steel will have high ductility after low-temperature treatments, become brittle within a narrow intermediate-temperature range, and regain ductility after higher-temperature treatments.
Temper embrittlement has previously been documented in conventional tempered martensitic steels without systematic ductility recovery in the higher-temperature regime.
Transition temperatures and timescales are sensitive to alloying content and impurity levels.
Insufficient diffusion-mediated recovery can prevent re-entrant ductility.
Impurity concentrations below a threshold can prevent observable embrittlement.
